abstract: |
  Financial fraud detection is an extreme imbalanced-learning problem. The fraudulent records form a tiny fraction of the total activity, yet the cost of missing them is high. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) such as the TabPFN family and different versions of TabICL have recently matched gradient-boosted decision trees on tabular classification through in-context learning, predicting by conditioning on a labelled context at inference time rather than by training a model per dataset. The context window is bounded, and under heavy class imbalance the standard practice of filling it by uniform random subsampling spends almost the whole window on redundant legitimate records while admitting only a handful of fraud examples. Such a context has two candidate deficiencies, irrelevance and class imbalance. This thesis proposes and evaluates Retrieval-Augmented Prediction (RAP), a test-time strategy that retrieves a structurally similar context by k-nearest-neighbour search and rebalances it to a controlled fraud ratio, and decomposes its effect into the two levers through four context-construction conditions on frozen models. Five TFMs and two gradient-boosted baselines are evaluated on five public fraud datasets with fraud rates of 0.13 to 1.5 %, using prevalence-corrected PR-AUC and recall at fixed false-positive rates. Ratio control is the lever that works. Rebalancing a random context improves every model on every dataset, the optimum is a broad plateau near 10 % fraud, and without per-dataset tuning the rebalanced context is at par and above with methodologically sound published state-of-the-art results depending on the dataset. Retrieval is a negative result. Retrieved contexts never outperform random ones, degrade performance severely on some datasets, and the full RAP combination stays below plain rebalancing everywhere. An ablation attributes the damage mainly to the retrieved legitimate rows, which reduce the diversity of the negative class. Context construction is thus a real test-time lever for TFMs under heavy imbalance, but the effective end of it is the class ratio, not relevance.
